en: The Essentials for Daily Use in the Vinaya, compiled by the Bhikṣu Hongjie of Baohua Mountain. Read by Ti. Collected for Early Awakening.

(According to the common regulations of the Sūtras and Vinaya, ordained disciples must diligently pursue the Buddha-way during the first and last watches of the night, rather than indulging in sleep, laziness, or negligence; therefore, at the time of awakening, one should recite this verse.)
As one first awakens from sleep, may all sentient beings awaken to all-encompassing wisdom and survey the ten directions.

(When ringing the bell at dawn or dusk, approach the bell with sincere palms joined; after reciting this verse, you may then ring the bell with your hands, while either reciting the names and virtues of the Buddhas or the titles of Mahāyāna sūtras.)
Or recite secret mantras, so that all sentient beings, upon hearing the sound, may leave suffering behind and all attain liberation.
May this sound of the bell transcend the Dharma-realm, reaching even the dark depths of the Iron Ring Mountains;
may all hear it, and through the purification of the sense-object of hearing, realize perfect penetration, so that all sentient beings may achieve true awakening.
Upon hearing the bell (recite this verse and mantra whenever one hears the bell, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down):
Hearing the sound of the bell, Afflictions grow light, Wisdom increases, And Bodhi arises.
Departing from hell, Escaping the fiery pit, May we attain Buddhahood To deliver all sentient beings.
Oṃ karateye svāhā (recite three times).
(The Ancient Masters said:
"If one hears the bell and does not rise from bed, the Dharma-protecting deities will become angry, and one's merit and wisdom will diminish before one's eyes."

In future lives, one will fall into the body of a snake—this is the retribution for those who are lazy in practicing meditation and recitation (as detailed extensively in the Sūtras and Vinaya, I shall not cite them here at length).
Regarding wearing robes: whenever one puts on or changes robes, one should recite this verse for each individual garment; it does not mean that one recites it only once when first dressing at dawn.
When putting on the upper garment, one should wish that all beings obtain supreme roots of goodness and reach the further shore of the Dharma.
When putting on the lower skirt, one should wish that all beings clothe themselves in all roots of goodness and be fully endowed with shame and remorse.
When arranging the robes and fastening the belt, one should wish that all beings restrain their roots of goodness so as not to let them be lost or scattered.
Placing the Order (snap the fingers three times; silently recite this verse and mantra):
From the morning dawn until evening, may all sentient beings protect themselves.
If any should lose their lives beneath my feet, I pray that you be reborn immediately in the Pure Land.
Oṃ. Ete tiṣṭhantu svāhā. (Recite three times.
When walking without harming insects, as one lifts the foot, may all sentient beings be born from the ocean of birth and death and be endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
Oṃ dhiri dhiri svāhā (three times). When exiting the hall from the residence,
one should wish that all sentient beings may deeply enter the Buddha’s wisdom and forever transcend the triple world.

Regarding entering the latrine (when one intends to defecate or urinate, one should go immediately; do not wait until the internal pressure becomes urgent and one is forced to act in haste). One must remove and change one’s footwear; one must not enter the latrine wearing clean shoes.

Upon arrival, one should snap the fingers three times. This has two purposes: first, to inform those inside that one is present, so as not to press them to leave; second, out of fear of foul-dwelling spirits, so as to cause them to avoid the area. When ascending the stool, one should again snap the fingers three times and silently recite this verse-mantra.
When defecating or urinating, one should wish that all sentient beings abandon greed, hatred, and delusion, and eliminate all unwholesome dharmas.
Oṃ hulu dāya svāhā. (After finishing the defecation, recite this verse and mantra while at the water to perform purification.)
When the task is finished and one approaches the water, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings swiftly proceed within the supramundane Dharma.
Oṃ śrī-vāhe svāhā (recite three times). [This purifies defilements.]
Washing away physical impurities, I vow that all sentient beings shall be pure, harmonious, and supple, ultimately free from defilement.
Oṃ ha na mi li ti svāhā. (Recite three times; wash with the ring finger of the left hand.
Washing the hands.
Washing the hands with water, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain pure hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Oṃ. Jvalāya svāhā. (Recite three times.

(If only urinating, it is sufficient to wash the hands once with water to be purified. If defecating, after removing the impurity, wash the hands using ash, mud, or soap pods, cleansing according to the Dharma. [From the *Xitang Zalu*, Yuan Dynasty].)

During the Zhongyou era, there was a monk from Shu named Dharma Master Zhichao who had been reciting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra for thirty years. One day he encountered a youth of refined appearance who raised his hand in a formal salutation. Zhichao asked, "Where have you come from? The youth replied, "From Mount Wutai. Zhichao asked, "Why have you traveled so far to reach here?

The youth said, "I wish to guide you regarding a minor matter. Zhichao said, "I would like to hear it. The youth replied, "It is truly praiseworthy that our master recites the sūtra; however, there is a lapse in your practice: when you enter the latrine to wash yourself clean, the foul water from your cleansing drenches your back of the hand."

Yet he had never used ash and water to wash them. According to the Vinaya regulations, ash and water should be applied seven times; nowadays, however, it is done only two or three times. Because of this, residual defilement remains, and thus one incurs an offense for every prostration to the Buddha or recitation of the sutras.

Having finished speaking, he vanished. Fubao was ashamed and reformed his ways. Those who understood remarked, "This must have been a manifestation of Mañjuśrī to warn Fubao. Therefore, one knows that washing the hands must be performed according to the Dharma. The *Caiguo jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) says: "If one uses defiled hands to request a sutra, one shall receive the retribution of becoming an insect in a latrine."
Washing the face with water, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the gateway of the pure Dharma and be forever free from defilement.
Oṃ bala svāhā. (Recite silently twenty-one times.)
When the Buddha drank water, he beheld eighty-four thousand insects within a single bowl; had he not held this mantra,
it would have been as if he were eating the flesh of sentient beings.
Oṃ vastraparamaṇi svāhā (three times). Five robes (in Sanskrit: *antarvāsa*;

here translated as "work robe"; five strips, one long and one short. Whenever performing labor or service within the monastery, or when entering and exiting on the road, one should wear this robe and recite this verse-mantra.
The *Jie tan jing* states: "The five strips symbolize the severing of greed and the purification of bodily karma").
Excellent is this robe of liberation, the supreme garment of the field of merit. I now receive it upon my head;
may I never be parted from it in life after life. Oṃ siddhya svāhā. (Recite three times.)

The Seven-Robed Garment (Sanskrit: *uttarāsaṅga*; Chinese: *rù zhòng yī*, meaning "garment for entering the assembly"; consisting of seven strips, with two long and one short). Whenever attending a meal, listening to lectures, reciting scriptures, practicing seated meditation, prostrating to the Buddha, prostrating to stupas, prostrating to one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or senior monks, or when the monastic community assembles, one should wear this garment and recite this verse and mantra.
The Seven-Robed Garment symbolizes the severing of anger and the purification of verbal karma.
Excellent is this robe of liberation, the supreme field of merit garment. I now receive it upon my head;
may I always wear it throughout all lifetimes.
Oṃ, tūṣṇīṃ tūṣṇīṃ svāhā. (Recite three times.)

The *saṃghāṭī* (Sanskrit; here translated as "variegated robe" or *zàsuìyī*). There are nine grades of this robe, ranging from superior to inferior: the lowest of the low grade has nine strips (*navaka*), the middle of the low grade has eleven strips, and the highest of the low grade has thirteen strips.

In all cases, there are two long [sections] and one short. The middle-low grade has fifteen sections; the middle-middle grade has seventeen sections; the middle-high grade has nineteen sections—all of which have three long and one short. The lower-high grade has twenty-one sections; the upper-middle grade has twenty-three sections; and the upper-upper grade has twenty-five sections—all of which have four long and one short.

Because the number of long sections increases while the short sections decrease, this symbolizes the increase of the holy and the decrease of the mundane. Thus, when entering royal palaces, ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, entering villages to beg for food, or subduing non-Buddhists, [the robe should be worn accordingly].
When wearing these robes, recite this verse-mantra to signify the severing of delusion and the purification of one’s intention:
Excellent is the garment of liberation, The robe of the unsurpassed field of merit. Upholding the Tathāgata’s command, I shall extensively deliver all sentient beings.
Oṃ mahābāva ṭasite svāhā (recite three times). Regarding the practice of covering these three robes while designating them as a "field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*), the *Zenghui ji* states:

Just as a field of irrigated plots stores water to grow fine seedlings that nourish the physical life, so too the field of the Dharma-robes is moistened by the waters of the four benefits, increasing the seedlings of the three virtues to nourish the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body.

The *Zangyi jing* states that there are ten kinds of benefits of the *kāṣāya*: first, it is the foremost for attaining Bodhi; second, it is honored among the multitudes of humans and devas; third, parents prostrate themselves before it; fourth, it is like a lion...

1. Sacrificing one’s body; 2. Dragons shedding their scales to escape calamity; 3. Kings showing reverence and faith; 4. Sentient beings prostrating; 5. Rākṣasas paying respect; 6. Devas and nāgas providing protection and aid; 7. Attaining the path of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that when the Buddha made his vows before the Buddha Ratnagarbha, he prayed: "When I attain Buddhahood, may my *kāṣāya* possess five merits. First, those who enter my Dharma—even if they have committed grave offenses or hold false views—shall, within their thoughts, feel reverence and honor it."

1. One will certainly receive the prediction of attaining one of the three vehicles (*tripitaka-yāna*). 2. Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and others who can show even a small measure of respect toward this *kāṣāya* robe shall immediately attain non-retrogression in the three vehicles.

3. If any ghosts, spirits, or humans obtain even four inches of the *kāṣāya*, they will have their food and drink sufficiently provided. 4. When sentient beings are at odds with one another, if they bring the *kāṣāya* to mind, compassion will immediately arise within them. 5. If one holds even a small portion of it and treats it with reverence and respect, one will always surpass others. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "That the sons of the Śākya accept and uphold the prohibitive precepts is their nature;

that they shave their hair and dye their robes is their mark. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Wherever you dwell, you must always be accompanied by the three robes (*tricīvara*), just as a bird’s two wings are constantly with its body. You [must not] abandon them..."

One’s own lineage is such that one has left the household life out of faith; it should be thus. Wherever one goes, the Dharma robes must accompany the person; one should not stay overnight separated from them. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the Buddha said:

"A bhikṣu’s three robes and one bowl must always be carried with him. One who violates this incurs an offense upon crossing the boundary. One should revere the three robes as if they were a stūpa. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the Buddha said: "Guard the three robes as you would your own skin; guard the bowl as you would your eyes.

Wherever you travel, go together with the robes and bowl, without any lingering attachment, just like a flying bird. If one enters a village or a layperson's dwelling without carrying the three robes, one commits an offense. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one must carefully guard the three robes as if they were the thin skin of the body; they must always be carried with one like the feathers of a bird, whether flying or walking.

According to the Mahāyāna Brahmajāla Bodhisattva Precepts, the Buddha said: "If a son of the Buddha, one should constantly practice *dhūta* during the two seasons; sit in meditation during winter and summer; observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*); and always use tooth-sticks, cleansing powder, the three robes, a water flask, an alms bowl, and a sitting mat."

The iron staff, incense burner, water filter, hand towel, knife, fire-starter, tweezers, rope bed, and the scriptures, Vinaya, images of the Buddha, and images of Bodhisattvas—these eighteen items must always accompany the person when a Bodhisattva practices *dhūta* austerities or travels abroad, whether journeying for a hundred or a thousand *li*.

To be without them constitutes an offense. Indeed, the three robes and one alms bowl are what every Buddha personally maintained and every Patriarch transmitted; they are observed by all seven classes of followers and prescribed for both vehicles. If one says [they are unnecessary]...

We are disciples of the Buddha; robes and alms bowls may be set aside. Regarding the fact that the regulations differ between the eastern and western lands, I request that you consult the Tripiṭaka: which sūtra, which vinaya, and which śāstra permits such [practices]? You should know that the words of the Buddha are trustworthy, whereas ordinary speech has no authority.
Those with wisdom should not be defiled by heterodox winds, but must instead strengthen their power of faith. Thus it is said.

Bedding (Sanskrit: *niṣīdana*; here translated as "sitting mat"; also called "cloth for sitting according to [the occasion]" or "cloth for lining the feet"). It is two and a half *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha in length and two *vitasti* in width. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

One span (*vitasti*) of the Tathāgata is two feet and four inches; this is calculated according to the small cubit (*kṣudra-vitasti*). If measured by the large cubit (*mahā-vitasti*), it may be reckoned as two feet. It must not be used for the three robes (*tricīvara*); it must not be given away as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), nor taken to carry firewood, grass, or miscellaneous items.

It may only be used as a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). When traveling on a journey, one may take it with them to sit upon at their destination. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The new [mat] shall have two layers; the old, four layers. One should not accept a single-layered *niṣīdana*. This original regulation in the Vinaya was established for the sake of the body and the robes.

Regarding the purpose of the bedding (niṣīdana): The *Sìchāo* states: First, for the sake of the body, it is because one fears that sitting directly on the ground might cause injury. Second, for the sake of the robes, it is because one fears that the three robes (*tricīvara*) might be damaged due to lack of protection. Third, for the sake of the bedding itself, it is because one fears that bodily impurities might defile the monastic beds and seats.

The Vinaya states: "When making a new *niṣīdana*, one should use the scraps from the old one to border its four edges so as to blend their colors; when making one, one should install such borders. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "Cut it into three parts, with the long end remaining as one part; then patch the four corners, or omit this if preferred.

In the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* and the *Nanhai Jìguì Zhōngfǎ Tǒngzì* (Record of the Inner Law Sent Home from the Southern Seas), it is not permitted to use it for prostrations or for spreading out as a mat. In the five regions of India, such usage is rarely seen or heard of. As for the practice in this land (China) of using it for prostrations and spreading it out, it is unknown when this tradition began. As...

Following the sacred regulations, this [practice] is not considered standard. However, if one discusses it as a formal robe, there is no hindrance to performing prostrations while wearing it. This has been explained in detail herein; students may proceed according to their convenience.
Reclining mat and sitting cloth, nurturing the sprout of the mind’s nature; Unfurling them to ascend the ground of the sages, I uphold the Tathāgata’s command.
Oṃ, dāna-pāda dāna-pāda svāhā. (Recite three times.)
Ascending the site of enlightenment,
if one should behold the Buddha, one should then wish that all sentient beings obtain unobstructed eyes and see all Buddhas.
Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ (recite three times).
I praise the Buddha, the Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, Peerless throughout the three realms, The Teacher of gods and humans,
the compassionate father of the four modes of birth. Now I take refuge for a moment in him, Who can extinguish the karma of three great kalpas.
To praise or extol him, even for billions of eons, one could never reach the end;
among gods and men in heaven and earth, there is none like the Buddha, and throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is no equal.
I have seen all that exists in the world; there is no one like the Buddha. [Recite] the Universal Homage Mantra:

Oṃ Vajra Hūṃ. (Recite three times; prostrate three times. One must practice this visualization with sincere devotion, casting down the five limbs. It is essential to know the seven types of prostrations taught therein. First: the prostration of pride, which refers to following the order of rank.)

1. Prostration with a lack of reverence: The mind wanders toward external objects and the five limbs (of the body) are not properly aligned; it is like the up-and-down motion of a pestle. 2. Prostration of chanting and responding: This refers to a coarse and formal demeanor where the mind lacks meditative reflection. Upon seeing someone, one prostrates hastily with a light body; once the person has left, the body collapses and the mind becomes exhausted.

This is merely the mouth chanting while the mind is distracted. 3. Prostration of reverence of body and mind: This means that upon hearing the name of a Buddha being chanted, one immediately brings the thought of that Buddha to mind. With body and mind in a state of reverence, one practices with diligence, free from weariness or indolence. 4. Prostration of the purity of awakened wisdom:

This means realizing the realm of the Buddhas as it manifests according to the mind’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To prostrate to one Buddha is to prostrate to all Buddhas; to perform a single bow is to prostrate to the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because the Buddha’s Dharma-body is all-pervasive and interfused. 5. Prostration of universal entry into the Dharma-realm: This means observing one's own body [as identical to the Dharma-realm].

The dharmas of the mind and so forth have, from the very beginning, not been separate from the *dharmadhātu*. The Buddha and the self are equal. To now prostrate to one Buddha is to universally prostrate to all Buddhas of the *dharmadhātu*. Sixth is the prostration of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). This means prostrating to one’s own Buddha and not relying on another Buddha. Why?

Because all sentient beings each possess Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), which is the equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Seventh is the prostration of the equality of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). This means that previously there was the act of prostrating and the object of contemplation, with self and other being two distinct things.

Now, in this single prostration, there is neither self nor other; ordinary beings and sages are as one, and the function of prostration is non-dual. Thus Mañjuśrī said: "The nature of the prostrator and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent. The first three [types of prostration] pertain to phenomena (*dharma*), while the latter four concern principle (*tattva*). In the *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*, the śrāvaka Jñānapradīpa asked Mañjuśrī: "How..."

"What is the manner of worshipping the Buddha? Mañjuśrī replied: "If one perceives the purity of the Dharma, this is called perceiving the purity of the Buddha. Whether body or mind, neither bowing nor rising, remaining upright and stable, unmoving and unshakable, with a tranquil mind and practicing tranquil conduct—this is called worshipping the Buddha.

A bhikṣu must not worship the Buddha while wearing the *kaṣāya* over both shoulders; if he dies, he will fall into the Iron Armor Hell. Exceptions are when sitting in meditation or receiving food; in these cases, wearing it over both shoulders is not an offense. A bhikṣu must not wear the meditation robe (*cīvara*) while worshipping the Buddha, reciting sutras, walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), paying respects to elders, or proceeding before stupas and temples.

Upon death, he will be transformed into a species such as a ball-fish, a tortoise, or a soft-shelled turtle. Furthermore, he must not cover his head; he must expose his crown. One who violates this incurs an offense, except during times of illness or extreme cold. This applies to all those who have left the household life with right faith."
Regarding those who receive the precepts at home, one must be extremely careful.

As for the offering of the *kundikā* (Sanskrit; here translated as "vase"; the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states there are two types: first, those made of ceramic or earthenware for pure use; second, those made of copper or iron for contact use;

what is explained here is the pure-use vase), every morning at dawn, after the bhikṣu has finished reciting the sūtras and mantras, he uses the pure vase to fill it with clean water and places it before the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. When he wishes to draw water from the vase, he should perform the visualization of the Buddha and Bodhisattva.
The Venerable One assumed his majestic appearance. Having performed the prostrations according to the ritual and arisen, he took up the flask and silently recited this verse-mantra.
Holding the pure flask in hand, one should make this aspiration for all sentient beings:
May they be free from defilement both within and without, And may they all be rendered radiant and pure. Oṃ śālagarucchaṅkha svāhā. (Recite three times.)

The Mantra for Cleansing the Vase: (Having prostrated to the Buddha and arisen, take an empty vase to the place where pure water is kept. With the left hand, lift up the edge of your robe; with the right hand, hold the vase.
Slowly draw water first and rinse it three times, reciting this mantra seven times each time. Do not pour the rinsing water back into the pure water; you must discard it outside.)
Oṃ. [Klaṃ] Svāhā (twenty-one times).
The Mantra for Pouring Water (once the vessel has been cleansed of all dust, fill it with pure water and silently recite this mantra).
Oṃ vaśit-pramāṇi svāhā (recite three times).

[Approach the Buddha, kneel on the right knee, hold the flask with the left hand, and form the mudrā of universal offering with the right hand. Recite the Great Compassion Mantra seven times, prostrate, and withdraw. At the end of the evening, emerge from the water. Form the mudrā as before.

First recite the Great Compassion Mantra seven times, the Heart Sūtra, and the Rebirth Mantra seven times each. Go outside and sprinkle water upon a clean spot. Form the Amṛta Mudrā with the hands and silently recite the Amṛta Dhāraṇī.]
Namo surūpāya tathāgatāya. Tadyathā: Oṃ suru suru prasu ru prasuru svāhā. (Recite three times.
While reciting, visualize the flask as a wish-fulfilling vessel (*cintāmaṇi-ghaṭa*) from which various kinds of food and drink flow forth.

First, the devas; next, the spirits (*yakṣas*); and finally, the hungry ghosts (*pretas*), animals (*tiryagyonis*), and others, each obtaining full satisfaction. Furthermore, visualize the flask producing multi-storied pavilions (*kūṭāgāras*), palaces, and precious jewels.

Adorned with necklaces, holding parasols and canopies, and bearing incense, flowers, and robes—all fully provided—he then expounded the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and conferred upon him the Three Refuges. Having caused him to hear the Dharma and receive the refuges, he attained the Samādhi of Dharma-Joy, prostrated himself, and departed.

Receiving Food (The bhikṣu receives food; he sits cross-legged, spreads his cloth napkin over his knees—fearing that rice, soup, vegetables, or broth might fall upon his kāṣāya—and when requesting the bowl, he silently recites this verse).

If one sees an empty bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings ultimately attain purity, being empty and free from afflictions (*kleśa*). [Note: *Pātra* (Sanskrit); here translated as "measured vessel.

According to the Vinaya, it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to possess bowls made of various precious materials, bronze, tin, wood, stone, or the like. In general, there are two types: first, clay; second, iron. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"The bowl is the utensil of those who have left the household life. It is for those with few desires and contentment; it is not suitable for worldly people. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: 'The bowl is the insignia of all Buddhas. It must not be used for evil purposes nor for washing hands; one should revere it as one's own eyes. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: [The Buddha]..."]

One should fashion one’s own bowl-mold to serve as a model for future ones. Furthermore, the *Fayin chaoyao* states: "It is a vessel that accords with the Dharma. This refers to three aspects—substance, color, and capacity—all of which must correspond to the Dharma. Regarding substance, there are two types: clay and iron.

Regarding color, one uses crushed sesame seeds and bitter almonds to coat both the interior and exterior, then treats it by smoking with bamboo smoke until it takes on the color of a pigeon's neck or peacock feathers. Why is it smoked? Because in summer, such a bowl does not corrode when holding food and does not become stained with grease;

since it possesses these functional benefits, it must be treated with smoke. Regarding capacity, there are three grades: superior, middling, and inferior. According to the Chinese *dou*, the superior bowl holds one *dou*, the middling bowl seven and a half *sheng*, and the inferior bowl five *sheng*. Therefore, it is called a "vessel of appropriate measure. Master Daguan said: "The bowl..."

As for its function as a vessel: it supports the Three Jewels and is replete with the six virtues. How is this support of the Three Jewels made clear? It is because, were it not for this [vessel], the Sangha would have no means of sustenance. If the Sangha has no means of sustenance, the life-force of wisdom (prajñā-jīvita) will be severed. If the life-force of wisdom is severed, the lineage of the Buddha (buddha-vaṃśa) will perish.

If he is able to be pure, able to be receptive, able to be frugal, able to be expansive, able to be honorable, and able to be ancient, these are what are called the six virtues. The ancient was bestowed by the Buddha; the honorable was presented by the heavens; the expansive universally benefits all; and the frugal means not eating beyond moderation.

As for its appearance, it receives offerings both refined and coarse, yet its blessings and benefits are impartial. As for its purity, no one in the world would dare to cast pungent foods into it. For these reasons, how could we, our humble selves, not cherish and revere it? When serving rice, silently recite this verse.
If you see a bowl full, you should wish that all sentient beings be fully replete with all wholesome dharmas.

(When performing the visualization for the offering: lean the right hand against the rim of the bowl to block its vapors; hold the bowl with the left hand level with the eyebrows; turn the bowl and spoon outward; complete the visualization for the offering. Then place the bowl on the table. To generate the food:
take seven grains of rice with the spoon—no larger than an inch of dough—and form the Amṛta-mudrā with the left thumb pressing the ring finger. Silently recite the verse:)

Regarding the *Chusheng* (Birth): [The tradition has been transmitted uniformly that when reciting for the morning meal, one should contemplate the inconceivable power of the Dharma; at the midday meal, one should contemplate the Great Garuda Bird. However, reasoning from this principle, it does not matter whether it is the morning meal, the small meal, or the midday meal—whenever one recites for the offering of food, one must maintain both verses simultaneously.
Only then can it accord with the original intent. Otherwise, there is a danger of falling into partiality or descending into what is contrary to the Dharma.]
The power of the Dharma is inconceivable; compassion is without obstruction. Seven grains pervade the ten directions, universally bestowed throughout the entire realm of dust.
(Give the rice from the spoon to the attendant to deliver. Hold the spoon facing inward and silently recite the mantra:)
Oṃ. Tuo liyi svāhā. (Recite the mantra three times; snap the fingers three times.
The Great Garuda, the hosts of wilderness spirits, the rākṣasas, and the Mother of Ghosts—may they all be filled with nectar.
Oṃ. Muḥ te svāhā. (Recite the mantra three times; snap the fingers three times.

Nowadays, I frequently observe those who use hand gestures (*mudrā*) to represent Mount Sumeru, circling the food several times, or perhaps, having finished the circumambulation, flipping their hand gestures about, performing all manner of such antics. Upon examining the *sūtras* and *vinaya*, none of these practices appear in the canonical texts; they completely lose the dignity of proper decorum. If one were to discuss the correct principle, it is simply this:

bind the seal with the left hand alone, take the food with the right hand, and silently recite the verses and mantras within the mouth—this is what is authentic. According to the *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Inner Dharma Sent Back from the Southern Seas), when the monastic community of the Western Regions arrives at the place where offerings are received for a meal, they first...

Set out a seat for the Holy Sangha (āryasaṃgha). Beside it, set out a small table and place a basin upon it to offer to Hārītī. Whenever food is distributed, first offer it to the Holy Sangha, next to the assembly present here, and finally offer food to Hārītī.

There is no rule requiring that separate portions be produced for each; however, following ancient customs of this Eastern land, although separate portions may be produced, one must not engage in various elaborate fabrications.
The attendant has sent food for you,
the assembly of ghosts and spirits; I now offer this sustenance to you, that this food may be shared by all ghosts and spirits throughout the ten directions.
Oṃ. Mūliṅ svāhā. (Recite three times. The attendant returns with the food. The *vinaya-dhara* chants the *saṃgha-bhadra*: The Buddha ordained that bhikṣus maintain five reflections while eating.
If the mind is distracted and filled with idle chatter, it will be difficult to digest the faithful offerings.

When the assembly hears the sound of the bell, each should maintain right mindfulness. [In the Vinaya, regarding the Buddha’s ordinance for the Saṃgha to chant the *saṃgha-bhadra* when receiving food: Because non-Buddhists once invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha and secretly placed poison in the food, the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to...

They chant in unison: *Sambhāradatta*. All poisonous substances are transformed into exquisite, delicious flavors; the assembly eats in peace and security, escaping the harm of poison. Regarding the term *saṃgha-bhāṣya*: *saṃgha* refers to the community of monks who receive the food; *bhāṣya* refers to the secret mantra being recited.

The Sanskrit *sambhāradatta* means "equal offering" (*sam-bhāra*), because the food for the assembly of monks is equal. It is also called "well-arrived" (*su-saṃprāpta*), meaning that the offerings are well-prepared and the meal arrives at the proper time.

Now, in this land, one recites the five reflections while eating to cause the assembly to receive the food with a single mind. This serves as the *saṃgha-bhāṣya* for two reasons: first, to prevent the harm of non-Buddhist poisons; second, to cause people to receive the food with a sense of shame and humility. Therefore, although it is not a formal regulation, it is practiced.
(Widely practiced in the Eastern Lands).
Holding the alms-bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings become accomplished vessels of the Dharma and receive the offerings of devas and humans.
Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ (recite three times; hold the bowl at the chest while receiving food; take three spoonfuls with proper intervals).
(First Spoon) May I vow to sever all evils. (Second Spoon) May I vow to cultivate all virtues. (Third Spoon) I vow to deliver all sentient beings.

(A practitioner who acts thus, by the power of these vows and mantras, offers more than the seven treasures filling the Ganges River and food and drink of a hundred flavors to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Sages and Worthies. [Do not violate the Five Contemplations].)
First, calculate the amount of labor expended and measure the distance from which the food has come. Second, assess one's own virtuous conduct to determine whether one is worthy of such offerings.

Third, guard the mind against transgressions, making the elimination of greed and other afflictions the primary principle. Fourth, regard the meal as a wholesome medicine intended to treat the withered body.
Five. One should accept this food for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path. (1) Calculating the labor involved:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that from the time this food is sown, harvested, threshed, ground, sifted, boiled, and finally prepared, the effort expended is immense. One should measure its origin; the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the donor reduces their own and their wife and children’s portions to give it away for the sake of seeking merit.

Whenever one receives food, one should form this reflection. (2) Weighing one’s own virtue and conduct against the requirements for being worthy of offerings: The *Vinayamātṛkā-vinaya* states that if one does not practice seated meditation, recite the scriptures, or attend to the affairs of the Triple Gem...

If one does not uphold the precepts yet accepts the faithful offerings of others, one will fall because of wealth; therefore, it is improper to accept food. If one’s virtuous conduct is complete, then one may rightfully receive offerings and eat. Whenever receiving food, one should perform this contemplation:

the three ways of guarding the mind to remain free from faults, with the cessation of greed and other afflictions as the primary principle. The *Vyākhyāyukti-ṭīkā* states: "A renunciant must first guard against three faults of the mind: namely, giving rise to greed for superior flavors, giving rise to anger toward inferior flavors, and giving rise to delusion regarding middling flavors. Because of this, one fails to know shame or remorse and falls into the three evil realms.

Whenever receiving food, one should perform this contemplation. Fourth, regarding food as excellent medicine: it is for the purpose of treating the emaciation of the physical form. This means that hunger and thirst are the primary diseases, while the four hundred and four ailments are secondary diseases; therefore, one must take food as medicine.

To sustain the body, whenever one receives food, one should form this contemplation: Regarding the four hundred and four diseases, the human body is a temporary composition of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind. If even one of these elements becomes unbalanced, one hundred and one types of disease arise;

when all four elements are combined, they constitute the four hundred and four diseases. Fifth, for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path, one should accept this food. This means that if one does not eat, the afflictions of hunger and thirst will arise; how then can the work of the Path be accomplished? The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"Eating too much leads to suffering and affliction; eating too little causes the decline of physical strength. One who eats in moderation is like a scale with no rising or falling. Whenever one receives food, one should form this contemplation.
Before concluding the meal, first recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī. Next, recite this verse:
"Those who practice giving Will surely obtain its benefit; If one gives for the sake of happiness, One will later attain peace and joy."
When the meal is finished, one should wish that all sentient beings accomplish all that they have to do and be endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas.
With this water used for washing the bowl, which possesses a flavor like celestial ambrosia, may it be bestowed upon all the spirits and deities.
May all obtain full satisfaction. Oṃ maheśvara-svāhā (three times).
Spread the bowl.
The Tathāgata is the vessel of measure; now I have obtained the opportunity to unfold [this practice].
May I, together with all the assembly, be empty and quiescent in the three spheres. Oṃ sma-maṇi svāhā. (Recite three times.)
The two types of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—and their acceptance are equal and without distinction; this constitutes the perfection of *dānapāramitā*.

[Then] one takes a *yángzhī* (in the Vinaya, these are called *dantakāṣṭha*, or tooth-sticks). There are four kinds of *yáng* trees, all of which may be used for cleaning the teeth: first, the white *yáng*, with round leaves; second, the green *yáng*, with long leaves; third, the red *yáng*, whose leaves turn red when the frost descends.

Fourth, the *huángyáng* (yellow ash) tree. By nature it is hard and dense, making it difficult to grow. Nowadays, willow twigs are universally used as substitutes for *yángzhī* (tooth-sticks). Because willow twigs hang downward, they are actually a minor variety of ash. If one were in a place where there are no willows, what would one use to clean the teeth?

One must know that all types of wood may be used to clean the teeth; all are called *chìmù* (dental wood). One simply takes a type with a mild nature and a bitter taste and chews it; it does not refer exclusively to the single species of willow wood.
Holding a *śalākā* (tooth-stick), one should wish: "May all sentient beings attain the wondrous Dharma and reach ultimate purity.
Oṃ sarvadhātu-sattva-sarva-tarima-sarvadhātu-stambha oṃ laṃ svāhā. (Recite this Mantra for Purifying the Dharmadhātu twenty-one times.)
When chewing the *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick), one should make this aspiration:
"May the minds of all sentient beings be harmonized and purified, and may they devour all afflictions. Oṃ amogha-mīmāle īvākara-saṃśuddhaye padma-kumāra.
RAḤ. EVAṂ SAṂSTUTĀYA. DHARA DHARA. SUMI MĀṄKHA SVĀHĀ (three times). (Whenever one chews a tooth-stick, one must ensure all saliva has been cleared away before rinsing with water;

one must not comb one's teeth while holding water in the mouth. There are five benefits to chewing a tooth-stick: first, the mouth does not become bitter; second, the mouth does not become foul-smelling;

third, it removes wind disorders; fourth, it removes heat disorders; fifth, it removes phlegm and mucus. If the remains are used, they should be discarded in a secluded place and must not be thrown where the assembly walks or sits.)

Rinse the mouth, rinse the mouth; even the mind is purified. The water kissed by the lips bears the fragrance of a hundred flowers. With the three karmas ever pure, go together with the Buddha to the Western Land.
Oṃ haṃ. Oṃ haḥ svāhā (three times). Take out the *khakkhara* (Sanskrit: *khakkhara*; Chinese: *xizhang*;

held by the Buddhas of the three periods to manifest the merit of wisdom and conduct, and to purify afflictions and karmic obstructions). After the bhikṣu has finished his morning meal and used the tooth-stick, he must prostrate to the Buddha and take out the staff.

If there is a layperson (*avadātavasana*) or a *śrāmaṇera*, have them hand it to him. If there is no one, after prostrating three times to the Buddha and rising, he should take it himself and go outside. Facing east, he should wipe away the dust according to the Dharma.

Perform the visualization. Regarding the ritual conduct of this visualization, it is detailed at length in the *Śalākā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Alms-staff) concerning the time when one takes up the staff with the hand, silently reciting this verse-mantra:
Holding the alms-staff, I vow that all sentient beings shall establish great assemblies of giving and reveal the path of reality. Oṃ. Nṛtya nṛtya nṛtyapate nṛte naya bhaṇe hūṃ.
Phaṭa (three times).
When spreading out a mat to sit in meditation, or when arranging a seat or couch, one should wish: May all sentient beings unfold wholesome dharmas and perceive the true mark of reality.
Sitting upright with body straight, one should wish that all sentient beings sit upon the seat of Bodhi with minds free from attachment.
Oṃ vajra-anipralani-ityaya svāhā (recite three times). Regarding sleep:
when about to sleep, join the palms facing west, visualize and recollect the Buddha ten times, or a hundred thousand times, or ten thousand times; having done so, recite the verse as follows:
When resting and sleeping at the proper time, one should wish that all sentient beings attain peace and stability of body and that their minds be free from agitation and distraction.

(Visualize the wheel of the letter *A*. Recite it twenty-one times in a single breath, then lie down. One must lie on the right side; this is called "auspicious sleep. One must not lie on the back, nor on the stomach, nor on the left side.
One must not remove one's inner garment or undergarment before lying down. One should maintain mindfulness of one’s original object of practice.)

Regarding the water filter (Sanskrit: *parisrāvaṇa*; Chinese: lǜ shuǐ luó; "water-strainer for filtering water"): In the Vinaya, after the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had established the precepts, they did not know how to make a water filter. The Buddha permitted one shaped like a ladle.

Whether it be triangular, or made into a large basin, or made into a water-strainer, if one suffers from the emergence of insects, it is permitted to place sand inside a bag. One must not discard it on dry land; it should be returned and placed back into the water. The *Huìzhèngjì* states: "If making a bag, fine, well-woven silk is best.

If fine silk is unavailable, fine cotton cloth may also be used. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When examining the water, one should not examine it with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), nor should one have someone with impaired vision examine it.

Even one who can see the fine lines on the palm of the hand may examine it. It should not be too quick, nor should it be too long; it should be like the time it takes for a great elephant to turn its head once. If there are extremely minute organisms in the water, one must not use that water to wash one's hands or face, or for the performance of the major or minor bodily functions."

The *Menjing xun* (Instructions for Gatekeepers) states: "The water filter is an instrument for practicing compassion and a condition for aiding sentient beings. Great conduct arises from this; the ultimate Way is realized through it. Whenever one draws water, recite these verses and mantras of the names and virtues of all Buddhas;
the merit will be boundless. This may truly be called upholding the precepts."
If you see flowing water, you should wish that all sentient beings obtain wholesome intentions and wash away the defilements of delusion.
Homage to the Buddha King of Joyful Adornment. Homage to the Tathāgata Jewel Topknot.
Homage to the Buddha King of Immeasurable Victory.
Oṃ vaśiparamaṇi svāhā (three times).
If one sees a great river, one should wish that all sentient beings may enter the stream of the Dharma and penetrate the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.
If one sees a bridge or a path, one should wish that all sentient beings may extensively deliver all others, just like a bridge.
Bathing the Buddha:
I now bathe all the Tathāgatas, the mass of merit adorned by pure wisdom;
may the sentient beings of the five turbidities be freed from defilement and together realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Praising the Buddha and his marks and signs of excellence, one should wish that all sentient beings may accomplish the Buddha-body and realize the signless Dharma. Oṃ. Muni muni samantamune svāhā.

Circumambulating the Stūpa (In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is said that when paying homage to the Buddha, one must not be like a mute sheep. Furthermore, when paying homage to a Buddha-stūpa, one should circumambulate by keeping the right side toward it, just as the sun, moon, and stars revolve around Mount Sumeru;

one must not circumambulate by keeping the left side toward it. There are five matters regarding circumambulation: first, keep the head bowed and gaze at the ground; second, do not step on insects; third, do not look to the left or right; fourth, do not sleep on the ground; fifth, do not converse with others. Furthermore, one obtains five blessings:

first, in future lives, one will obtain a handsome and upright appearance; second, one will obtain a beautiful voice; third, one will be reborn in the heavens; fourth, one will be born among kings and nobles; fifth, one will attain the path of Nirvāṇa).
Circumambulating the stūpa clockwise, one should wish that all sentient beings act without opposition and achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
*Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ dupa dupa svāhā.* (Recite three times. Regarding the care of the sick:

according to the Vinaya regulations, only those endowed with five virtues are permitted to attend to the sick. First, they must know what the patient may or may not eat; if it is permissible to eat, they should provide it. Second, they must not treat the patient’s excrement, urine, mucus, or vomit with contempt or disdain.

Third, they possess a heart of compassion and do not act for the sake of food or clothing. Fourth, they are able to manage medicines until the patient recovers or passes away. Fifth, they are able to preach the Dharma to the sick person, thereby increasing their own merit in wholesome dharmas; thus, even if they tend to the patient’s suffering for no long time, [the benefit is great].
Whenever one sees [a sick person], one should immediately recite this verse-mantra. Among the eight fields of merit, nursing the sick is the foremost field of merit).
Upon seeing a person who is ill, one should make this aspiration for all sentient beings:
May they realize that the body is empty and quiescent, And may they depart from the dharma of discord and strife. Oṃ śrīda śrīda kumtāre svāhā. (Recite three times.)

Shaving the Head (The days for shaving the head compiled by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: the fourth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, nineteenth, and twenty-second of each month).
Twenty-three. Twenty-four. Twenty-five. Twenty-six. Twenty-nine. (Recite this verse-mantra silently):
Having shaved off hair and beard, I vow that all sentient beings May distance themselves from afflictions And attain ultimate quiescence.
Oṃ siddhantu mantrāḥ bhadraye svāhā. (Recite three times.)

Regarding bathing (according to the Vinaya regulations for bhikṣus: one may bathe once every half-month, but not more frequently, except during times of illness, heat, labor, wind, rain, or while traveling on a road; these circumstances are not restricted). Furthermore, when bathing, one should choose the appropriate day.

Those days to be avoided are the six *poṣadha* days. On these days, the various devas descend to the human realm to observe the good and evil deeds of people; therefore, one should cultivate goodness and perform virtuous acts. The so-called six *poṣadha* days are the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, [twenty-ninth, and thirtieth] of each month.

29. 30. Whenever entering the bathhouse, one should hang clean clothes on the clean pole and contaminated clothes on the contaminated pole. One must not relieve oneself in the bathhouse; one must not converse or laugh with others; and one must not wash in secluded spots.

If one has sores or scabies, it is appropriate to bathe last. If there are particularly fearsome sores, one should still avoid them to prevent pricking people's eyes. (Recite this verse and mantra silently.)
While bathing the body, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings be free from defilement of body and mind, Radiant and pure within and without.
Oṃ vajranirghātana svāhā. (Recite three times.
Then wash the feet.
When washing the feet, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings be endowed with the power of the divine feet, so that their movements are unimpeded.
Oṃ Āḥ Svāhā" (recite three times). The Characteristics of the Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera.

(There are two kinds of śrāmaṇeras: first, those who resemble śrāmaṇeras in form; second, those who resemble śrāmaṇeras in dharma. If one has only undergone tonsure and ordination but has not yet received the categories of precepts, they are called a śrāmaṇera in form.

If one has received the tenfold pure precepts, they are called a śrāmaṇera in dharma. Within the category of those resembling śrāmaṇeras in dharma, there are further three types: from seven to thirteen years of age, they are called *kūka-śrāmaṇeras* (crows-driving śrāmaṇeras); from fourteen to nineteen, they are called *dharmānurūpa-śrāmaṇeras* (dharma-conforming śrāmaṇeras); and from twenty years of age upward, they are called *nāmamātra-śrāmaṇeras* (nominal śrāmaṇeras).)
First, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from stealing; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct;
fourth, abstaining from false speech; fifth, abstaining from drinking intoxicants;
sixth, abstaining from wearing perfumes, garlands, and ointments on the body.
Seventh: not to engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor to intentionally go to observe or listen to them;
eighth: not to sit upon high, wide, or large beds; ninth: not to eat at improper times; tenth:
not to handle or possess raw gold, silver, or precious objects.
A śrāmaṇera should possess five virtues; one should know this from the *Daśasaṃkhyāpuṇyakṣetra-sūtra*.
It says: "A śrāmaṇera should know five virtues. The first is that he has resolved to leave the household life, cherishing and wearing the Way within his breast."
Second, they mar their physical appearance in order to wear the dharma-robes. Third, they sever their affections and bid farewell to their kin so as to be free from partiality.
Fourth, they cast aside their bodies and lives in order to honor and revere the Way. Fifth, they resolve to seek the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering all beings.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One should explain the ten categories to a śrāmaṇera: first, all sentient beings depend upon food and drink; second, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

third, the knowledge of the three feelings (*vedanā*); fourth, the four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*); fifth, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*); sixth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatanāni*);

seventh, the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-bodhyaṅgāni*); eighth, the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*); ninth, the nine abodes of sentient beings (*nava-sattvāvāsāḥ*); tenth, [the ten wholesome paths of action].
The ten bases of totality (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*).
The ten precepts for *śrāmaṇerī*s (as above, not listed again).
The precepts for *śikṣamāṇā*s.

(Vaṃśī-mānāpikā; here translated as "female trainee in the precepts"). The Buddha permitted that a woman who had previously been married for ten years, or a maiden of eighteen, be granted two years of training (*śikṣamāṇā*) to purify her body through the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*) and to purify her mind.

Within the community of nuns, a formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) is conducted before the assembled assembly. Only after she has completed these twelve years of training and reached twenty years of age may she receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). If the years of training have not been fulfilled or the six rules have not been purified, she shall not be granted the full ordination of a bhikṣuṇī.
First, refrain from sexual misconduct; second, refrain from stealing; third, refrain from killing;
fourth, refrain from false speech; fifth, refrain from eating at improper times; sixth, refrain from drinking intoxicants.

(According to the Vinaya regulations, for the *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī*—the three lower assemblies—one should maintain two upper robes. One is the *uttarāsaṅga*, which is a seamless robe (*sāṃghāṭī*) and not one made of cut and sewn patches.)

This refers to the *saṃghāṭī* robe. The alms bowl he carries is a copper vessel; it is not a standard *pātra* bowl. At our current mountain monastery, for anyone from eighteen years of age down to seven who wishes to receive the śrāmaṇera precepts, they must, according to the Vinaya regulations, prepare two *kaṣāya* robes with uncut strips (*sāṃghāṭī*) to wear and carry.

If one is twenty years of age or older and comes to request the full ordination (*upasampadā*), the three robes they have prepared must all be made of cut-and-sewn patches (*khaṇḍa-saṃsṛṣṭa*) and the bowl must be of the proper measure.

Even if they lack the uncut-strip robes, it is permitted by expedient means to receive the ten śrāmaṇera precepts, wear them, and practice them. There are two reasons for this: first, so that their full ordination will not be distant, as the śrāmaṇera precepts serve as the foundation for the bhikṣu precepts; second, because the robes and requisites are difficult to obtain, [this is intended] to ensure...

Because seeking a *man-yi* (unsewn robe) conversely becomes a cause and condition for obstructing the precepts, I clarify this matter in advance so that those who study the Vinaya may know it was established by the Buddha; it is not intended to display eccentricity or delude the masses. Furthermore, in the old versions, the characteristics of the five categories of offenses for *bhikṣus* were listed after the characteristics of the *śrāmaṇera* precepts;

these have now been deleted and removed. They are appended following the "Correct Model for the Poṣadha of the Two Vehicles. This is because the Buddha prohibited *śrāmaṇeras* and laypeople from knowing the characteristics of the five categories of offenses, fearing that they might become obstructed upon receiving full ordination and thus incur the fault of being a "thief-dweller" (*caura-vāsa*).
The characteristics of the Upāsaka precepts are:
first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct;
fourth, not speaking falsehoods; and fifth, not drinking intoxicants.

(Regarding these five precepts: if one is unable to receive them in their entirety, one may instead undertake one, two, three, or four precepts; the Buddha’s compassionate skillful means permits each such case. However, if one is a person of sincere faith and wisdom, only by fully observing all five precepts does one constitute a true reception.)
The precepts of the Eightfold Fasting Observance (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) are:
first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, not speaking falsehoods;
fifth, not drinking intoxicants; sixth, abstaining from flowers, perfumes, and necklaces, and from anointing the body with fragrant oils.
7. Abandoning high, large, or luxurious beds, as well as singing, dancing, music, and performances, and going to watch or listen to them;

8. Abandoning eating at improper times (*vikālabhojana*). (The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Now, the essence of the fast (*upoṣadha*) consists in not eating after midday. Eight matters assist in establishing the essence of the fast, supporting one another; this is called the 'Eight-Limbed Fast' (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), also known as the 'Eightfold Observance Fast' (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇa-upavāsa*). The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:)

Why is it that only the avoidance of these eight matters is taught? These eight matters serve as the gateway; through these eight precepts, one abandons all evil. Among them, the first four are actual evils, while drinking alcohol is the gateway to all evils. The remaining three are so designated because they can give rise to the causes and conditions that obstruct the Path.

By means of these eight dharmas, the five vehicles are perfected. "Guan" (the gate) refers to the closing off of all evils. These eight precepts may be observed for a single day and night, or on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, or on the six *caidai* (fasting) days.

Regarding the six *caidai* days, they correspond to what was explained previously in the section on bathing. Alternatively, they may be observed on the birthdays of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or on one's own birthday; these are all suitable occasions for undertaking them. The treatise states: "If one receives the eight precepts, one should do so for one day and one night."

At night, do not allow these to be confused with the lifelong precepts. These eight precepts may be received by anyone, regardless of whether they have already received the five precepts or the lay bodhisattva precepts. Lately, among those who have shaved their heads and left the household life, many receive and uphold the eight precepts; even their teachers claim to bestow the five or eight precepts upon them.
Yet, they fail to investigate the Vinaya teachings thoroughly, yet take pleasure in acting as teachers for others. Thus, both the blind lead the blind, and all that they do is incorrect.

Now, at this mountain monastery, if any who have left the household life come to request the reception of the eight precepts, or wish to don the five or seven patched robes (*kāṣāya*), none shall be permitted. Furthermore, regarding the lay *upāsaka* and *upāsikā* precepts, the Buddha’s regulations do not permit the wearing of the patched *puṇyakkhetta* robe; he commanded—

To don the robes for ritual repentance, prostrate before the Buddha, and recite the sutras refers specifically to the *man-yi* (the loose-fitting robe). This is because the two groups of lay followers were instructed by the Buddha to provide offerings to the Triple Gem according to their own means; they were not permitted to receive the four requisites from others. Since they were not fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for sentient beings, [they did not require such robes].

Therefore, it is not permitted to wear the patched *kṣetra-patram* (field-robe). Furthermore, even if one has received the lay Bodhisattva precepts, one must store the three robes, the alms bowl, and the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) to offer before the Buddha.

Whenever one encounters ordained monks or nuns who lack their robes and requisites, or those of full age who wish to receive full ordination but lack robes and bowls, one should give them whatever is requested and then create new ones for offering. One must certainly store these items. As for oneself, one is permitted to wear a single piece of seamless cloth (*sāṇa-vastra*) while performing prostrations and recitations;

however, it is not permitted to wear it while traveling through cities or villages. If one enters a monastery to pay homage to the Triple Gem, it should be kept in a bag and carried with one, to be worn only once inside the monastery grounds. Thus, for a layperson, it is permitted to be separated from one's robes; if one wears them constantly, one violates the regulations. For the ordained, this is not the case.

It is not permitted to be separated from one’s robes; if one is separated, it constitutes a violation of the regulations. Now, at this mountain monastery, whenever there are laymen or laywomen of faithful heart who request to receive the five precepts or the bodhisattva precepts, they are required to provide *maṇḍala* (unsewn) robes for the purpose of paying homage to the Triple Gem.

It is not permitted to wear the *kāṣāya* with its vertical stripes or the field-patterned robe. Furthermore, the specific characteristics of the bodhisattva precepts are not listed here within the *Daily Practice of the Vinaya*; they are appended in the middle of the volume on the *Correct Model for the Poṣadha*.
